records.source: Ἐν ἐκείναις ταῖς ἡμέραις πάλιν πολλοῦ ὄχλου ὄντος καὶ μὴ ἐχόντων τί φάγωσιν, προσκαλεσάμενος τοὺς μαθητὰς λέγει αὐτοῖς·
records.gloss: In those the days again great crowd being and not having what they might eat, having called to [him] the disciples he says to them,
pieces: During those days a large crowd had gathered again, and there was no food for them. So Jesus called {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and said to them,

L.1: In those days, when again [there] was a great crowd and they had nothing to eat, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} called the disciples to [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}] and says to them,

R.1: Around that time another big crowd came together around Jesus. The people had run out of food. So Jesus called {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} followers over and said to them,

decisions.choice: again a great crowd: a second large crowd, like the one in 6:34
decisions.reason: The word for again points back to the earlier feeding. Mark tells a second, similar meal in a different place, the Gentile region of the Ten Towns where Jesus was in 7:31.

decisions.choice: again a great crowd, the reading of the SBLGNT
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts read a single word meaning a very great crowd, without again. The SBLGNT reads again with great, as the older manuscripts do. Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: says: present tense in a story about the past
decisions.reason: Mark often tells past events in the present tense to make them vivid. The sense is past, here and in 8:6, 8:12, 8:17, 8:19-20, 8:22, 8:29 and 8:33.

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Jesus at the start of a new section.

records.heading: Seven loaves in a deserted place

records.source: Σπλαγχνίζομαι ἐπὶ τὸν ὄχλον ὅτι ἤδη ἡμέραι τρεῖς προσμένουσίν μοι καὶ οὐκ ἔχουσιν τί φάγωσιν·
records.gloss: I have compassion on the crowd, because already days three they remain with me and not they have anything they might eat;
pieces: "My heart goes out to these people. They have been with {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} for three days now, and they have nothing left to eat.

L.2: "I have compassion on the crowd, because they have already remained with {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} three days and do not have anything to eat;

R.2: "I feel sorry for these people. They have stayed with {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} for three days, and now they have nothing to eat.

decisions.choice: have compassion: be moved deep inside with pity
decisions.reason: The verb comes from the word for the inner parts, where people felt strong feeling. It is used of Jesus at 1:41 and at the first feeding (6:34).

decisions.choice: already three days: they have stayed so long that their food is gone
decisions.reason: The point is how long they have kept listening to him in a lonely place.

decisions.choice: my heart goes out to
decisions.reason: Balanced uses a natural English phrase for deep pity.

records.source: καὶ ἐὰν ἀπολύσω αὐτοὺς νήστεις εἰς οἶκον αὐτῶν, ἐκλυθήσονται ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ· καί τινες αὐτῶν ἀπὸ μακρόθεν ἥκασιν.
records.gloss: and if I send away them hungry to [the] home of them, they will faint on the road; and some of them from far away have come.
pieces: Send them home without food, and they will collapse on the road. Some of them have traveled a long way."

L.3: and if I send them away hungry to their homes, they will faint on the road; and some of them have come from far away."

R.3: If they have to go home hungry, they will become weak and fall down on the way. Some of them have come from far away."

decisions.choice: faint: give out from weakness and hunger
decisions.reason: The verb means to become slack or exhausted.

decisions.choice: from far away: perhaps a hint that Gentiles are among the crowd
decisions.reason: The scene is in Gentile country (7:31), and in the Scriptures those far off can mean the nations (Joshua 9:6; Isaiah 60:4). Mark may mean no more than the distance.

decisions.choice: and some of them, the reading of the SBLGNT
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts join the clause with a word meaning for, making it a reason. The sense is close either way. Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

records.source: καὶ ἀπεκρίθησαν αὐτῷ οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ ὅτι Πόθεν τούτους δυνήσεταί τις ὧδε χορτάσαι ἄρτων ἐπ’ ἐρημίας;
records.gloss: And answered him the disciples of him that, From where these will be able anyone here to satisfy with bread in a desolate place?
pieces: His disciples replied, "Out here in this empty country, where could anyone find bread enough to fill all these people?"

L.4: And {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples answered {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "From where will anyone be able to satisfy these [people] with bread here in a desolate place?"

R.4: His followers answered, "We are far from any town. How could anyone get enough bread here to feed all these people?"

decisions.choice: desolate place: open country far from towns
decisions.reason: The same word is used for the lonely place of the first feeding (6:35). It recalls Israel fed in the wilderness (Exodus 16).

decisions.choice: a question that sees no way to feed them
alternatives: a request for Jesus to act
decisions.reason: The disciples have seen the first feeding (6:35-44), yet they speak as though they had not. Jesus takes this up in 8:17-21.

decisions.choice: we are far from any town
decisions.reason: Readable says what the lonely place means for the problem.

records.source: καὶ ἠρώτα αὐτούς· Πόσους ἔχετε ἄρτους;
records.gloss: And he was asking them, How many have you loaves?
pieces: He asked them, "How many loaves have you got?"

L.5: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} asked them, "How many loaves do you have?"

R.5: Jesus asked them, "How many loaves of bread do you have?"

decisions.choice: loaves: small flat rounds of bread
decisions.reason: Bread was baked in small, flat rounds, one or two of which made a meal for a person.

records.source: οἱ δὲ εἶπαν· Ἑπτά.
records.gloss: And they said, Seven.
pieces: "Seven," they answered.

decisions.choice: seven: a number of fullness
alternatives: a count with no further meaning
decisions.reason: The first feeding began with five loaves and ended with twelve baskets. Here there are seven loaves and seven baskets (8:8). Seven can stand for completeness, but Mark gives no explanation.

records.source: καὶ παραγγέλλει τῷ ὄχλῳ ἀναπεσεῖν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς· καὶ λαβὼν τοὺς ἑπτὰ ἄρτους εὐχαριστήσας ἔκλασεν καὶ ἐδίδου τοῖς μαθηταῖς αὐτοῦ ἵνα παρατιθῶσιν καὶ παρέθηκαν τῷ ὄχλῳ.
records.gloss: And he directs the crowd to recline on the ground; and having taken the seven loaves, having given thanks he broke and was giving to the disciples of him that they might set before, and they set before the crowd.
pieces: He had the crowd sit on the ground. Taking the seven loaves, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} gave thanks, broke them, and kept handing them to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples to pass around, and they served them to the crowd.

L.6: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} directs the crowd to recline on the ground; and having taken the seven loaves [and] given thanks, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} broke [them] and was giving [them] to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples so that they would serve [them], and they served the crowd.

R.6: Jesus told the people to sit on the ground. He took the seven loaves and thanked God for them. Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} broke the bread into pieces and gave it to {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} followers to hand out. They gave it to the people.

decisions.choice: recline: sit or lie down to eat
decisions.reason: People lay or sat on the ground for a meal, as at the first feeding (6:39-40).

decisions.choice: took, gave thanks, broke, gave: the same actions as at the Last Supper
decisions.reason: Mark uses the same series of verbs at the first feeding (6:41) and at the Last Supper (14:22-23). The word for giving thanks is the one used of the cup at 14:23.

decisions.choice: was giving: he kept handing the bread out
decisions.reason: The imperfect tense describes repeated action as the bread kept coming.

decisions.choice: thanked God for them
decisions.reason: Readable names God, to whom the thanks were given.

records.source: καὶ εἶχον ἰχθύδια ὀλίγα· καὶ εὐλογήσας αὐτὰ εἶπεν καὶ ταῦτα παρατιθέναι.
records.gloss: And they had small fish a few; and having blessed them he said also these to be set before.
pieces: They also had a few small fish. He blessed them and told the disciples to hand those out too.

L.7: And they had a few small fish; and having blessed them, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to serve these also.

R.7: They also had a few small fish. Jesus thanked God for the fish and told {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} followers to give them out too.

decisions.choice: blessed them: gave thanks to God over the fish
decisions.reason: In a Jewish blessing at a meal, God is praised for the food. To bless the food means to give thanks for it.

decisions.choice: small fish: little fish, perhaps dried or salted
decisions.reason: The word is a diminutive. Small fish were often dried or pickled around the lake.

decisions.choice: thanked God for the fish
decisions.reason: Readable says what blessing the food means, as in 8:6.

records.source: καὶ ἔφαγον καὶ ἐχορτάσθησαν, καὶ ἦραν περισσεύματα κλασμάτων ἑπτὰ σπυρίδας.
records.gloss: And they ate and were satisfied, and they took up left over of broken pieces seven large baskets.
pieces: Everyone ate and had plenty. Then they collected the leftover pieces, enough to fill seven large baskets.

L.8: And they ate and were satisfied, and they took up what was left over of broken pieces, seven large baskets.

R.8: All the people ate as much as they wanted. Then the followers picked up the pieces that were left. They filled seven big baskets.

decisions.choice: large baskets: big woven baskets or hampers
decisions.reason: This is a different word from the basket of 6:43 and 8:19. It names a larger basket, big enough to let a man down in it over a wall (Acts 9:25). Jesus keeps the two words apart in 8:19-20.

decisions.choice: satisfied: fed until full
decisions.reason: The same verb as in 6:42 and 8:4.

decisions.choice: large baskets (L, B); big baskets (R)
decisions.reason: The size is part of the meaning of the word. All three levels mark it so that readers can tell these baskets from those of 6:43.

records.source: ἦσαν δὲ ὡς τετρακισχίλιοι.
records.gloss: There were now about four thousand.
pieces: There were about 4,000 people.

decisions.choice: about 4,000: the whole crowd
decisions.reason: Unlike 6:44, the Greek here does not use the word for adult men. It simply counts the crowd.

decisions.choice: people
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add the noun that English needs. They use people, since the Greek gives no word for men here.

records.source: καὶ ἀπέλυσεν αὐτούς.
records.gloss: And he sent away them.
pieces: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} sent them on their way.

decisions.choice: sent away: dismissed the crowd to go home
decisions.reason: The same verb as in 8:3. Now they have eaten and can go home.

records.source: καὶ εὐθὺς ἐμβὰς εἰς τὸ πλοῖον μετὰ τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ ἦλθεν εἰς τὰ μέρη Δαλμανουθά.
records.gloss: And immediately having embarked into the boat with the disciples of him he came into the parts of Dalmanutha.
pieces: At once {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} boarded the boat with {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples and came to the area of Dalmanutha.

L.10: And immediately {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} got into the boat with {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples and came into the region of Dalmanutha.

R.10: Right away Jesus got into the boat with {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} followers. They went to a place called Dalmanutha.

decisions.choice: Dalmanutha: a place by the lake not known from any other source
decisions.reason: No other ancient writing names Dalmanutha, and where it lay is not known. It was most likely on the west shore of the lake, in Jewish territory, since Pharisees meet Jesus there (8:11).

decisions.choice: Dalmanutha, the reading of the SBLGNT
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts read Magadan or Magdala, the names found in the manuscripts of Matthew 15:39. Scribes probably replaced an unknown place with a known one. Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: a place called Dalmanutha
decisions.reason: Readable signals that Dalmanutha is a place name.

records.source: Καὶ ἐξῆλθον οἱ Φαρισαῖοι καὶ ἤρξαντο συζητεῖν αὐτῷ, ζητοῦντες παρ’ αὐτοῦ σημεῖον ἀπὸ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, πειράζοντες αὐτόν.
records.gloss: And went out the Pharisees and began to argue with him, seeking from him a sign from the heaven, testing him.
pieces: The Pharisees came out and started to dispute with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. They demanded a sign from heaven, to put {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to the test.

L.11: And the Pharisees went out and began to argue with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, seeking from {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} a sign from heaven, testing {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.11: The Pharisees came out to argue with Jesus. They wanted to test {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, so they asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} for a sign from heaven to prove that God had sent {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: sign: a sign that would prove God was with him
decisions.reason: In Mark a sign is not one of Jesus' healings, which Mark calls works of power. It is a proof, given on demand, that God backs his claims. Israel asked such signs of God in the wilderness and was blamed for testing him (Psalm 95:8-9).

decisions.choice: from heaven: from God
decisions.reason: Heaven stands for God himself. The sign would come from the sky, but the point is that God gives it.

decisions.choice: testing: trying to trap him or prove him false
decisions.reason: The same verb is used of Satan's testing in 1:13. They want him to fail.

decisions.choice: sign
decisions.reason: Sign is a key term and keeps the same word at every level. Readable explains what the sign was meant to prove.

records.heading: No sign for this generation

records.source: καὶ ἀναστενάξας τῷ πνεύματι αὐτοῦ λέγει· Τί ἡ γενεὰ αὕτη ζητεῖ σημεῖον;
records.gloss: And having sighed deeply in the spirit of him he says, Why the generation this seeks a sign?
pieces: He groaned from deep within and said, "Why does this generation look for a sign?

L.12: And sighing deeply in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} spirit, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says, "Why does this generation seek a sign?

R.12: Jesus let out a deep groan and said, "Why do the people of today keep asking for a sign?

decisions.choice: sighed deeply: groaned from the heart
decisions.reason: The verb is stronger than the sigh of 7:34. It shows grief and frustration at their unbelief.

decisions.choice: in his spirit: in his own inner self
decisions.reason: This is Jesus' own spirit, the deepest part of him, as in 2:8.

decisions.choice: this generation: the people of this time, seen as unwilling to believe
decisions.reason: The phrase recalls the wilderness generation that tested God (Deuteronomy 32:5, 32:20; Psalm 95:10). It comes again in 8:38 and 9:19.

decisions.choice: the people of today
decisions.reason: Readable explains that the word means the people living now.

records.source: ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, εἰ δοθήσεται τῇ γενεᾷ ταύτῃ σημεῖον.
records.gloss: Truly I say to you, if will be given to the generation this a sign.
pieces: Truly I tell you, this generation will be given no sign at all."

L.12: Truly I say to you, no sign will be given to this generation."

R.12: I tell you the truth: God will not give them a sign. Never!"

decisions.choice: if ... a sign: an oath meaning certainly no sign will be given
decisions.reason: This is a Hebrew way of swearing an oath. The full form is "may God punish me if ...", which means "it will certainly not happen" (Psalm 95:11). Jesus denies the demand in the strongest terms.

decisions.choice: will be given: God is the unnamed giver
decisions.reason: The passive leaves God unnamed, as Jewish speech often did.

decisions.choice: no
decisions.reason: Even Literal gives the sense of the oath, since "if" alone would read as an unfinished sentence in English.

decisions.choice: God will not give them a sign. Never!
alternatives: no sign will be given to this generation
decisions.reason: Readable names God as the giver and shows the force of the oath with a separate word.

records.source: καὶ ἀφεὶς αὐτοὺς πάλιν ἐμβὰς ἀπῆλθεν εἰς τὸ πέραν.
records.gloss: And having left them, again having embarked he went away to the other side.
pieces: Leaving them, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} got into the boat again and went off to the far shore.

L.13: And leaving them, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} again got into [the boat] and went away to the other side.

R.13: Then Jesus left them. He got back into the boat and went across the lake.

decisions.choice: having left them: Jesus turns his back on the dispute
alternatives: he left them behind by accident
decisions.reason: Leaving them is his answer to their demand.

decisions.choice: the other side: the east shore of the lake
alternatives: another town on the same shore
decisions.reason: They cross back toward the north-east, where they reach Bethsaida (8:22).

decisions.choice: across the lake
decisions.reason: As in earlier chapters, Readable names the lake.

records.source: Καὶ ἐπελάθοντο λαβεῖν ἄρτους, καὶ εἰ μὴ ἕνα ἄρτον οὐκ εἶχον μεθ’ ἑαυτῶν ἐν τῷ πλοίῳ.
records.gloss: And they forgot to take loaves, and except one loaf not they had with themselves in the boat.
pieces: Now the disciples had forgotten to bring bread. They had just one loaf with them in the boat.

L.14: And they had forgotten to take loaves, and except for one loaf they did not have [any] with them in the boat.

R.14: Jesus' followers had forgotten to bring any food. They had only one loaf of bread with them in the boat.

decisions.choice: they: the disciples
decisions.reason: The disciples are with Jesus in the boat.

decisions.choice: one loaf: perhaps a hint that Jesus himself is the bread they have
alternatives: only a detail of the story
decisions.reason: Mark mentions the single loaf with care. Some read it as pointing to Jesus, who is with them in the boat. Mark does not say so.

decisions.choice: the disciples (B); Jesus' followers (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the subject, since the last people named are the Pharisees.

records.heading: Do you still not understand?

records.source: καὶ διεστέλλετο αὐτοῖς λέγων· Ὁρᾶτε, βλέπετε ἀπὸ τῆς ζύμης τῶν Φαρισαίων καὶ τῆς ζύμης Ἡρῴδου.
records.gloss: And he was instructing them saying, Watch, beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod.
pieces: He gave them a warning: "Be careful! Watch out for the Pharisees' yeast and Herod's yeast."

L.15: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was instructing them, saying, "Watch, beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod."

R.15: Jesus warned them, "Be careful! Watch out for the yeast of the Pharisees and of Herod."

decisions.choice: leaven: a bit of old fermented dough used to make new dough rise
decisions.reason: A small piece of old dough spread through a whole batch. In the Scriptures it often stands for a corrupting influence that spreads (1 Corinthians 5:6-8; Exodus 12:15).

decisions.choice: the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod: their unbelief and hostility
decisions.reason: Mark does not explain the picture. The Pharisees have just demanded a sign (8:11), and Herod killed John (6:14-29). The two groups plotted together against Jesus in 3:6. What they share is a refusal to see who Jesus is.

decisions.choice: Herod: Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee
decisions.reason: The same Herod as in 6:14-29.

decisions.choice: Herod, the reading of the SBLGNT
decisions.reason: A few manuscripts read "the Herodians", the party of 3:6. Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: yeast
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the everyday word. Readable keeps the picture, since the disciples' mistake in the next verses depends on it.

records.source: καὶ διελογίζοντο πρὸς ἀλλήλους ὅτι ἄρτους οὐκ ἔχουσιν.
records.gloss: And they were reasoning with one another that loaves not they have.
pieces: They began to talk it over among themselves: they had no bread.

L.16: And they were discussing with one another that they have no loaves.

R.16: The followers talked among themselves. They thought Jesus said this because they had not brought any bread.

decisions.choice: that they have no loaves: their talk was about having no bread
decisions.reason: The small word can give the content of their talk or its cause. Either way they think Jesus is speaking about real bread.

decisions.choice: they have, the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: we have, as their own words
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts add "saying" and read "we have", making it direct speech. The sense is the same. Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: they thought Jesus said this because
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that the disciples misunderstood the warning about yeast.

records.source: καὶ γνοὺς λέγει αὐτοῖς· Τί διαλογίζεσθε ὅτι ἄρτους οὐκ ἔχετε;
records.gloss: And having known he says to them, Why are you reasoning that loaves not you have?
pieces: Jesus knew what they were saying, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, "Why are you talking about having no bread?

L.17: And knowing [it], {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says to them, "Why are you discussing that you have no loaves?

R.17: Jesus knew what they were talking about. He said to them, "Why are you talking about not having bread?

decisions.choice: knowing it: he was aware of their talk
decisions.reason: Mark does not say how he knew. In 2:8 Jesus knows people's thoughts in his spirit.

decisions.choice: why: a rebuke, not a request for information
decisions.reason: This and the questions that follow scold the disciples for missing the point.

records.source: οὔπω νοεῖτε οὐδὲ συνίετε;
records.gloss: Not yet do you perceive nor understand?
pieces: Do you still not see it or understand?

L.17: Do you not yet perceive or understand?

decisions.choice: perceive, understand: the words of Isaiah 6:9-10, used of outsiders in 4:12
decisions.reason: In 4:12 Jesus used these words of those outside, who see but do not perceive. Now he asks whether his own disciples are in the same state.

decisions.choice: understand
decisions.reason: Readable joins the two verbs, which mean nearly the same, into one plain word.

records.source: πεπωρωμένην ἔχετε τὴν καρδίαν ὑμῶν;
records.gloss: Hardened have you the heart of you?
pieces: Have your hearts been hardened?

L.17: Do you have your heart hardened?

R.17: Are your hearts so hard that you cannot understand?

decisions.choice: hardened: dull and closed to understanding
decisions.reason: The heart is the place of thinking. Mark said this of the disciples after Jesus walked on the water (6:52), and of Jesus' opponents in 3:5.

decisions.choice: so hard that you cannot understand
decisions.reason: Readable says what a hard heart means here, as at 6:52.

records.source: ὀφθαλμοὺς ἔχοντες οὐ βλέπετε καὶ ὦτα ἔχοντες οὐκ ἀκούετε;
records.gloss: Eyes having not do you see, and ears having not do you hear?
pieces: You have eyes; can you not see? You have ears; can you not hear?

L.18: Having eyes, do you not see, and having ears, do you not hear?

R.18: You have eyes, but you do not see! You have ears, but you do not hear!

decisions.choice: eyes that do not see, ears that do not hear: the prophets' charge against Israel
decisions.reason: The words recall Jeremiah 5:21 and Ezekiel 12:2, where God's people have eyes and ears but will not use them. They also echo 4:9 and 4:12. The healings of a deaf man (7:31-37) and a blind man (8:22-26) stand on either side of this scene.

decisions.choice: statements instead of questions
decisions.reason: The questions expect the answer that they do not see or hear. Readable says this plainly.

records.source: καὶ οὐ μνημονεύετε ὅτε τοὺς πέντε ἄρτους ἔκλασα εἰς τοὺς πεντακισχιλίους, πόσους κοφίνους κλασμάτων πλήρεις ἤρατε;
records.gloss: And not do you remember, \v 19 when the five loaves I broke for the five thousand, how many baskets of broken pieces full you took up?
pieces: Do you not remember?
When I broke five loaves for the 5,000, how many baskets of leftover pieces did you gather?"

L.19: when I broke the five loaves for the 5,000, how many baskets full of broken pieces you took up?"

R.19: I broke five loaves of bread for 5,000 people. How many baskets of leftover pieces did you pick up?"

decisions.choice: do you not remember: read as running into the question of 8:19
alternatives: a separate question ending at the end of 8:18
decisions.reason: The SBLGNT punctuates 8:18 and 8:19 as one question. Some editions end the question at "remember". The sense does not change.

decisions.choice: baskets: the smaller baskets of the first feeding
decisions.reason: Jesus uses the word of 6:43 here and the word for large baskets in 8:20. Mark keeps the two feedings apart.

decisions.choice: I broke: Jesus names himself as the one who provided
decisions.reason: The point of the questions is who fed the crowds, and that he is with them in the boat.

decisions.choice: 5,000 people
decisions.reason: Readable adds people, as English needs a noun. In 6:44 the count was of men.

records.source: λέγουσιν αὐτῷ· Δώδεκα.
records.gloss: They say to him, Twelve.
pieces: "Twelve," they told {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: they say: present tense in a story about the past
decisions.reason: As in 8:1, the sense is past.

records.source: ὅτε καὶ τοὺς ἑπτὰ εἰς τοὺς τετρακισχιλίους, πόσων σπυρίδων πληρώματα κλασμάτων ἤρατε;
records.gloss: When the seven for the four thousand, of how many large baskets fillings of broken pieces you took up?
pieces: "And when I broke seven loaves for the 4,000, how many large baskets of pieces did you gather?"

L.20: "When [I broke] the seven for the 4,000, how many large baskets full of broken pieces did you take up?"

R.20: "And when I broke seven loaves for 4,000 people, how many big baskets of leftover pieces did you pick up?"

decisions.choice: when the seven for the 4,000: the verb broke is understood from 8:19
decisions.reason: Jesus repeats the question in short form for the second feeding.

decisions.choice: large baskets: the word of 8:8
decisions.reason: Jesus uses the same word for each meal that Mark used in telling it.

decisions.choice: I broke (L in brackets); loaves (B, R)
decisions.reason: English needs the verb and the noun that the short question leaves out.

records.source: καὶ λέγουσιν αὐτῷ· Ἑπτά.
records.gloss: And they say to him, Seven.
pieces: "Seven," they said.

decisions.choice: they say: present tense in a story about the past
decisions.reason: As in 8:19, the sense is past.

records.source: καὶ ἔλεγεν αὐτοῖς· Οὔπω συνίετε;
records.gloss: And he was saying to them, Not yet do you understand?
pieces: He said to them, "And you still do not understand?"

L.21: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to them, "Do you not yet understand?"

R.21: Then Jesus said to them, "And you still do not understand?"

decisions.choice: not yet understand: the disciples have seen but not grasped who Jesus is
alternatives: they do not understand the arithmetic
decisions.reason: The question is left open. The next scenes, the blind man healed in two stages (8:22-26) and Peter's confession (8:29), show their sight beginning to come.

decisions.choice: was saying: an imperfect, he said
decisions.reason: Mark often uses this form for Jesus' sayings. It does not change the sense.

records.source: Καὶ ἔρχονται εἰς Βηθσαϊδάν.
records.gloss: And they come to Bethsaida.
pieces: They came to Bethsaida.

R.22: Jesus and {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} followers came to the town of Bethsaida.

decisions.choice: Bethsaida: a fishing town at the north end of the lake
decisions.reason: Bethsaida lay just east of where the Jordan enters the lake. Philip the tetrarch had rebuilt it as a city, but Mark calls it a village (8:23). It was the town Jesus sent the disciples toward in 6:45.

decisions.choice: Jesus and his followers; the town of
decisions.reason: Readable names who came and says that Bethsaida is a town.

records.source: καὶ φέρουσιν αὐτῷ τυφλὸν καὶ παρακαλοῦσιν αὐτὸν ἵνα αὐτοῦ ἅψηται.
records.gloss: And they bring to him a blind [man] and implore him that him he might touch.
pieces: Some people brought a blind man to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and pleaded with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to touch him.

L.22: And they bring to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} a blind [man] and beg {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to touch him.

R.22: Some people brought a blind man to Jesus. They begged {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to touch the man.

decisions.choice: they bring: people of the town, not the disciples
decisions.reason: The subject is general, as in 7:32.

decisions.choice: touch him: people believed Jesus healed by touch
decisions.reason: Jesus had healed by touch many times (1:41; 5:41; 6:5; 7:33).

decisions.choice: some people
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make clear that others, not the disciples, brought the man.

records.source: καὶ ἐπιλαβόμενος τῆς χειρὸς τοῦ τυφλοῦ ἐξήνεγκεν αὐτὸν ἔξω τῆς κώμης, καὶ πτύσας εἰς τὰ ὄμματα αὐτοῦ, ἐπιθεὶς τὰς χεῖρας αὐτῷ, ἐπηρώτα αὐτόν· Εἴ τι βλέπεις;
records.gloss: And having taken hold of the hand of the blind [man] he led out him outside the village, and having spit on the eyes of him, having laid the hands on him, he was asking him, If anything you see?
pieces: He took hold of the blind man's hand and took him outside the village. Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} spat on the man's eyes, laid {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hands on him, and asked, "Can you see anything?"

L.23: And taking hold of the blind [man's] hand, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} led him out of the village, and when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had spit on his eyes [and] laid [{{deity_pronoun:his|His}}] hands on him, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} asked him, "Do you see anything?"

R.23: Jesus took the blind man's hand and walked with him out of the village. There {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} spit on the man's eyes and put {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hands on him. Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} asked, "Can you see anything?"

decisions.choice: spit on his eyes: saliva was thought to have healing power
decisions.reason: People in that world used saliva as a remedy. Jesus used it with the deaf man too (7:33). Here it is a touch of care.

decisions.choice: outside the village: Jesus heals him away from the crowd
decisions.reason: As with the deaf man (7:33), the healing takes place in private.

decisions.choice: if you see anything: a direct question
alternatives: an indirect question, he asked him whether he saw anything
decisions.reason: In questions of this time the word for if can introduce a direct question. The SBLGNT prints the words as Jesus' own.

decisions.choice: can you see
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable ask about the man's ability to see, which is the point of the question.

records.source: καὶ ἀναβλέψας ἔλεγεν· Βλέπω τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ὅτι ὡς δένδρα ὁρῶ περιπατοῦντας.
records.gloss: And having looked up he was saying, I see the men, for as trees I see walking.
pieces: The man looked up and said, "I see {{gender:people|men}}, but to me they are like trees moving about."

L.24: And looking up, he said, "I see {{gender:people|men}}, for I see [them] like trees, walking."

R.24: The man looked up and said, "I see {{gender:people|men}}! They look like trees that are walking."

decisions.choice: looked up: lifted his eyes, or began to see again
decisions.reason: The verb can mean to look up or to recover sight. Here he looks up and sees only in part.

decisions.choice: I see people, for I see them like trees: he knows they are people only because they move
decisions.reason: The shapes look like trees to him. He can tell they are people because they walk.

decisions.choice: people: human beings in general
decisions.reason: The word is the general word for human beings.

decisions.choice: but
decisions.reason: The small word here explains how he knows they are people. In English it reads more clearly as a contrast.

records.source: εἶτα πάλιν ἐπέθηκεν τὰς χεῖρας ἐπὶ τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς αὐτοῦ, καὶ διέβλεψεν καὶ ἀπεκατέστη καὶ ἐνέβλεπεν τηλαυγῶς ἅπαντα.
records.gloss: Then again he laid the hands on the eyes of him, and he saw clearly and he was restored, and he was seeing clearly all things.
pieces: Then Jesus laid {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hands on the man's eyes once more. The man looked hard, his sight came back, and he could see everything clearly.

L.25: Then again {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} laid [{{deity_pronoun:his|His}}] hands on his eyes, and he looked intently and was restored, and he saw everything clearly.

R.25: Then Jesus put {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} hands on the man's eyes again. The man looked carefully, and his eyes were healed. Now he could see everything clearly.

decisions.choice: a healing in two stages: a picture of the disciples, who see only in part
decisions.reason: This is the only healing in the Gospels done in two stages. It stands between the disciples' blindness (8:18) and Peter's confession, where Peter sees who Jesus is but not yet that he must suffer (8:29-33). Mark does not explain the link.

decisions.choice: looked intently: looked hard and saw through
decisions.reason: The verb means to see clearly or to stare. The man fixes his eyes and his sight comes back.

decisions.choice: restored: made as he had been
decisions.reason: The same verb as for the withered hand (3:5).

decisions.choice: he saw: he went on seeing
decisions.reason: The imperfect tense shows his sight lasted.

decisions.choice: Jesus (B, R); the man (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name each person, since the Greek uses he for both.

records.source: καὶ ἀπέστειλεν αὐτὸν εἰς οἶκον αὐτοῦ λέγων· Μηδὲ εἰς τὴν κώμην εἰσέλθῃς.
records.gloss: And he sent him to [the] home of him, saying, Not even into the village may you enter.
pieces: Jesus sent him off home, telling him, "Do not even set foot in the village."

L.26: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} sent him to his home, saying, "Do not even enter the village."

R.26: Jesus sent him home. He told him, "Do not even go back into the village."

decisions.choice: do not even enter the village, the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: do not enter the village nor tell anyone in the village
go to your home, and do not tell anyone in the village
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add or substitute "and do not tell anyone in the village", which makes plain the command to keep quiet found in 1:44, 5:43 and 7:36. The shorter reading is found in early manuscripts. Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: not even: he is to go straight home
alternatives: he may never return to the village
decisions.reason: Jesus keeps the healing quiet, as in 7:36. The man is not to pass through the village on the way.

decisions.choice: go back into
decisions.reason: Readable shows that the man came from the village.

records.source: Καὶ ἐξῆλθεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς καὶ οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ εἰς τὰς κώμας Καισαρείας τῆς Φιλίππου· καὶ ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ ἐπηρώτα τοὺς μαθητὰς αὐτοῦ λέγων αὐτοῖς· Τίνα με λέγουσιν οἱ ἄνθρωποι εἶναι;
records.gloss: And went out Jesus and the disciples of him into the villages of Caesarea of Philip; and on the road he was asking the disciples of him saying to them, Whom me do say the men to be?
pieces: Jesus and {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples set out for the villages of the Caesarea Philippi area. As they went, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} asked them, "Who do {{gender:people|men}} say I am?"

L.27: And Jesus and {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples went out into the villages of Caesarea Philippi; and on the way {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} asked {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples, saying to them, "Who do {{gender:people|men}} say that I am?"

R.27: Jesus and {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} followers went to the villages near the city of Caesarea Philippi. As they walked, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} asked them, "Who do people say I am?"

decisions.choice: Caesarea Philippi: a city at the foot of Mount Hermon, north of the lake
decisions.reason: Philip the tetrarch rebuilt the town and named it for Caesar. It was called Philip's to tell it apart from Caesarea by the sea. It lay in mostly Gentile country at the source of the Jordan.

decisions.choice: on the way: the road becomes the setting for Jesus' teaching
decisions.reason: From here to 10:52 Jesus teaches the disciples on the way to Jerusalem, and the word recurs (9:33; 10:32; 10:52).

decisions.choice: people: people in general
decisions.reason: The word is the general word for human beings.

decisions.choice: the villages of the area (B); the villages near the city of (R)
decisions.reason: The villages belonged to the area of the city. Readable adds that Caesarea Philippi was a city.

records.heading: You are {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}

records.source: οἱ δὲ εἶπαν αὐτῷ λέγοντες ὅτι Ἰωάννην τὸν βαπτιστήν, καὶ ἄλλοι Ἠλίαν, ἄλλοι δὲ ὅτι εἷς τῶν προφητῶν.
records.gloss: And they said to him saying that, John the Baptist, and others Elijah, others but that one of the prophets.
pieces: They answered, "Some say John the Baptist; some, Elijah; and others, one of the prophets."

L.28: And they told {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, saying, "John the Baptist; and others, Elijah; but others, one of the prophets."

R.28: They answered, "Some people say {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are John the Baptist. Others say {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are Elijah. And others say {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are one of the prophets."

decisions.choice: the same opinions Herod heard in 6:14-15
decisions.reason: The answers repeat the views of 6:14-15 almost word for word.

decisions.choice: Elijah: the prophet promised to return before the day of the Lord
decisions.reason: Malachi 4:5. See 6:15.

decisions.choice: some people say you are
decisions.reason: Readable writes each answer as a full sentence.

records.source: καὶ αὐτὸς ἐπηρώτα αὐτούς· Ὑμεῖς δὲ τίνα με λέγετε εἶναι;
records.gloss: And he was asking them, You but whom me do you say to be?
pieces: "And you," {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} asked them, "who do you say I am?"

L.29: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} asked them, "But you, who do you say that I am?"

R.29: Then Jesus asked them, "But what about you? Who do you say I am?"

decisions.choice: you: emphatic, set against people
decisions.reason: The pronoun stands first: but you, unlike them.

decisions.choice: he: emphatic, he himself
decisions.reason: Mark adds the pronoun as Jesus turns the question on the disciples.

records.source: ἀποκριθεὶς ὁ Πέτρος λέγει αὐτῷ· Σὺ εἶ ὁ χριστός.
records.gloss: Answering Peter says to him, You are the Christ.
pieces: Peter answered, "You are the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}."

L.29: Peter answers and says to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "You are the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}."

R.29: Peter answered, "You are the {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}, the King God promised to send!"

decisions.choice: the Christ: the Anointed One, the king God promised to send
decisions.reason: The word means anointed. Kings of Israel were anointed with oil, and the prophets promised a king from David's line who would set God's people free (2 Samuel 7:12-16; Isaiah 11:1-5). Mark used the title at 1:1.

decisions.choice: Peter's confession: the first time a disciple names Jesus as the Christ
decisions.reason: This is the turning point of Mark's Gospel. Peter sees who Jesus is, but the next verses show he does not yet see what kind of Christ he is (8:31-33).

decisions.choice: the King God promised to send
decisions.reason: Readable explains the title briefly.

records.source: καὶ ἐπετίμησεν αὐτοῖς ἵνα μηδενὶ λέγωσιν περὶ αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: And he warned them that no one they should tell about him.
pieces: He gave them strict orders not to tell anyone about {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.30: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} warned them that they should tell no one about {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.30: Then Jesus strictly told them not to tell anyone who {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was.

decisions.choice: warned: gave a stern command
decisions.reason: This is the same verb used for Peter rebuking Jesus and Jesus rebuking Peter (8:32-33), and for Jesus silencing demons (1:25; 3:12). Here it is a strict order.

decisions.choice: tell no one: the title must not be spread until its meaning is clear
decisions.reason: Jesus does not deny the title. People would hear it as a call to war against Rome. He begins at once to teach what kind of Christ he is (8:31).

records.source: Καὶ ἤρξατο διδάσκειν αὐτοὺς ὅτι δεῖ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου πολλὰ παθεῖν καὶ ἀποδοκιμασθῆναι ὑπὸ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων καὶ τῶν ἀρχιερέων καὶ τῶν γραμματέων καὶ ἀποκτανθῆναι καὶ μετὰ τρεῖς ἡμέρας ἀναστῆναι·
records.gloss: And he began to teach them that it is necessary the Son of Man many things to suffer and to be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes and to be killed and after three days to rise;
pieces: He then began teaching them that the Son of Man had to undergo great suffering, be rejected by elders, chief priests and scribes, be put to death, and rise again after three days.

L.31: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes and be killed and after three days rise again;

R.31: Then Jesus began to teach {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} followers. He said that the Son of Man must go through many terrible sufferings. The leaders of the people, the leading priests and the teachers of God's law would reject {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. He would be killed, but after three days {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} would come back to life.

decisions.choice: must: it is God's purpose, found in the Scriptures
decisions.reason: The word means it is necessary. In Mark the need comes from God's plan, written beforehand (9:12; 14:21, 14:49).

decisions.choice: rejected: the word of Psalm 118:22
decisions.reason: The same verb is used of the stone the builders rejected in Psalm 118:22, which Jesus quotes in 12:10.

decisions.choice: elders, chief priests, scribes: the three groups of the Jewish council in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Together they made up the Sanhedrin, the ruling council (14:53, 15:1). The chief priests were the high priest and leading priestly families.

decisions.choice: after three days: by the third day, counting in the Jewish way
decisions.reason: In Jewish counting part of a day counted as a day. Mark tells of the resurrection on the third day (16:1-2; compare 14:58, 15:29).

decisions.choice: the Son of Man: Jesus speaks of himself
decisions.reason: As in 2:10 and 2:28, Jesus uses the title for himself. It recalls the one like a son of man in Daniel 7:13-14.

decisions.choice: the leaders of the people
decisions.reason: Readable explains elders as leaders of the people, and uses teachers of God's law for scribes as in earlier chapters.

records.heading: The Son of Man must suffer

records.source: καὶ παρρησίᾳ τὸν λόγον ἐλάλει.
records.gloss: And openly the word he was speaking.
pieces: He spoke about this quite plainly.

L.32: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was speaking the word openly.

R.32: Jesus told them all this very plainly.

decisions.choice: openly: plainly, without hiding the meaning
decisions.reason: Until now Jesus has taught in parables and kept his identity hidden. Now he tells the disciples plainly.

decisions.choice: the word: this message about his suffering
decisions.reason: The phrase points back to what he has just taught in 8:31.

records.source: καὶ προσλαβόμενος ὁ Πέτρος αὐτὸν ἤρξατο ἐπιτιμᾶν αὐτῷ.
records.gloss: And having taken aside Peter him began to rebuke him.
pieces: Peter took {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to one side and began to rebuke {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.32: And Peter took {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} aside and began to rebuke {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.32: Then Peter took Jesus away from the others and began to tell {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was wrong.

decisions.choice: rebuke: speak sharply to correct
decisions.reason: The same verb as in 8:30 and 8:33. Peter speaks to Jesus as Jesus speaks to demons.

decisions.choice: taken aside: drew him away from the others
decisions.reason: Peter speaks to Jesus privately.

decisions.choice: tell him that he was wrong
decisions.reason: Readable uses plain words for rebuke.

records.source: ὁ δὲ ἐπιστραφεὶς καὶ ἰδὼν τοὺς μαθητὰς αὐτοῦ ἐπετίμησεν Πέτρῳ καὶ λέγει· Ὕπαγε ὀπίσω μου, Σατανᾶ, ὅτι οὐ φρονεῖς τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ ἀλλὰ τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων.
records.gloss: And having turned and having seen the disciples of him he rebuked Peter and says, Go behind me, Satan, because not you set your mind on the things of God but the things of the men.
pieces: But Jesus turned and looked at {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} rebuked Peter. "Get behind {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, Satan!" {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said. "Your mind is not on what God cares about, but on what people care about."

L.33: But turning around and seeing {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} rebuked Peter and says, "Get behind {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, Satan, because you are not setting your mind on the things of God but on the things of {{gender:people|men}}."

R.33: But Jesus turned around and looked at {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} followers. Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} rebuked Peter. "Get behind {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, Satan!" {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said. "You are thinking the way people think, not the way God thinks."

decisions.choice: get behind me, Satan: Peter is speaking for Satan and must take his place behind Jesus as a follower
alternatives: get out of my sight forever
decisions.reason: Satan tested Jesus in 1:13, and Peter's words test him to turn from suffering. Behind me is the word used in 1:17 and 8:34 for following. Jesus sends Peter back to the place of a disciple.

decisions.choice: seeing his disciples: the rebuke is for all of them
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks to Peter with the others watching, since they shared his thinking.

decisions.choice: set your mind on: to think and care about
decisions.reason: The verb covers both thinking and what one aims at.

decisions.choice: what God cares about ... what people care about
alternatives: the things of God ... the things of men
decisions.reason: "The things of" is vague in English. Balanced says what the things are, and "people" is already inclusive.

decisions.choice: thinking the way people think, not the way God thinks
alternatives: setting your mind on the things of God
decisions.reason: Readable turns the contrast into plain words and reverses the order for clarity.

records.source: Καὶ προσκαλεσάμενος τὸν ὄχλον σὺν τοῖς μαθηταῖς αὐτοῦ εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Εἴ τις θέλει ὀπίσω μου ἐλθεῖν, ἀπαρνησάσθω ἑαυτὸν καὶ ἀράτω τὸν σταυρὸν αὐτοῦ καὶ ἀκολουθείτω μοι.
records.gloss: And having called to [him] the crowd with the disciples of him he said to them, If anyone wants after me to come, let him deny himself and let him take up the cross of him and let him follow me.
pieces: Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} called the crowd over, together with {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples, and said to them, "If anyone desires to come after {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, they must say no to themselves, take up their cross, and follow {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

L.34: And calling the crowd to [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}] with {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} disciples, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to them, "If anyone wants to come after {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, let {{gender:them|him}} deny {{gender:themselves|himself}} and take up {{gender:their|his}} cross and follow {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

R.34: Then Jesus called the crowd and {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} followers to come near. He said to them, "If anyone wants to come with {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, they must stop living for themselves. They must be ready to carry their own cross and die, and they must follow {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

decisions.choice: deny himself: say no to oneself, give up the claim to run one's own life
decisions.reason: The same verb is used of Peter denying Jesus (14:30, 14:72). To deny oneself is to disown oneself in the same way, putting Jesus first.

decisions.choice: take up the cross: as a condemned man carried his cross to the place of death
decisions.reason: Rome made condemned men carry the crossbeam to their execution (15:21). The picture is of walking to one's death, ready to give one's life.

decisions.choice: anyone ... let him: a saying for every person
decisions.reason: The pronouns are masculine as Greek grammar requires, but the saying is for anyone in the crowd.

decisions.choice: the crowd with his disciples: the call to follow is for everyone
decisions.reason: Jesus calls the crowd in as well. The way of the cross is not only for leaders.

decisions.choice: they ... themselves ... their
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use they, themselves and their with anyone, a natural inclusive form in English, since the saying is for everyone. Literal gives the traditional form as a setting.

decisions.choice: be ready to carry their own cross and die
decisions.reason: Readable says what carrying a cross meant.

records.heading: Take up your cross

records.source: ὃς γὰρ ἐὰν θέλῃ τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ σῶσαι ἀπολέσει αὐτήν· ὃς δ’ ἂν ἀπολέσει τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ ἕνεκεν ἐμοῦ καὶ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου σώσει αὐτήν.
records.gloss: Whoever for if wants the life of him to save will lose it; whoever but will lose the life of him on account of me and the gospel will save it.
pieces: Anyone set on keeping their life safe will lose it, and anyone who loses their life because of {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} and the gospel will save it.

L.35: For whoever wants to save {{gender:their|his}} life will lose it, but whoever loses {{gender:their|his}} life on account of {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} and the gospel will save it.

R.35: Some people try hard to keep their life safe for themselves, but they will lose it. Others give up their life because of {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} and the good news. They will save it.

decisions.choice: life: the self, the life a person lives now and the life beyond death
alternatives: only the soul as distinct from the body
decisions.reason: The word means a person's life or self. In 8:35-37 it moves between this life, which may be lost, and the true life that God keeps. The same word is often rendered soul in 8:36-37; keeping one word lets the saying be heard as one.

decisions.choice: save, lose: a paradox about following Jesus
decisions.reason: Those who hold on to their life to keep it safe lose it in the end. Those who give it up for Jesus gain it in the end.

decisions.choice: on account of me and the gospel, the reading of the SBLGNT
decisions.reason: A few early manuscripts lack "me and". Reviewers should check this against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: their (B, R)
decisions.reason: As in 8:34, Balanced and Readable use their for a saying meant for anyone.

decisions.choice: two pairs of short sentences
decisions.reason: Readable breaks each half of the saying into its own sentences.

records.source: τί γὰρ ὠφελεῖ ἄνθρωπον κερδῆσαι τὸν κόσμον ὅλον καὶ ζημιωθῆναι τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ;
records.gloss: What for does it profit a man to gain the world whole and to forfeit the life of him?
pieces: What does anyone gain by winning the whole world, if it costs them their life?

L.36: For what does it profit {{gender:a person|a man}} to gain the whole world and forfeit {{gender:their|his}} life?

R.36: Suppose someone owned the whole world but lost their life. What good would that be to them?

decisions.choice: life: the same word as in 8:35, the self that may be lost forever
alternatives: soul as one part of a person
decisions.reason: The traditional rendering here is soul. The word is the one used for life in 8:35, and the loss meant is of the whole person before God.

decisions.choice: the world: everything people can own or win
decisions.reason: The point is the greatest possible gain.

decisions.choice: forfeit: lose as a penalty
decisions.reason: The verb is used of loss or damage paid as a penalty. It is the language of accounts: profit and loss.

decisions.choice: anyone (B); someone (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use inclusive words for a saying about any person.

records.source: τί γὰρ δοῖ ἄνθρωπος ἀντάλλαγμα τῆς ψυχῆς αὐτοῦ;
records.gloss: What for would give a man [as] exchange for the life of him?
pieces: What could anyone give to buy their life back?

L.37: For what would {{gender:a person|a man}} give in exchange for {{gender:their|his}} life?

R.37: What could a person give to get their life back? Nothing is worth that much!

decisions.choice: exchange: a price paid in return
decisions.reason: The word means something given in exchange. Psalm 49:8-9 says no one can pay God the price of a life.

decisions.choice: life: the same word as in 8:35-36
decisions.reason: Once a life is lost there is nothing anyone could pay to get it back.

decisions.choice: Nothing is worth that much!
decisions.reason: The question expects the answer nothing. Readable states it.

records.source: ὃς γὰρ ἐὰν ἐπαισχυνθῇ με καὶ τοὺς ἐμοὺς λόγους ἐν τῇ γενεᾷ ταύτῃ τῇ μοιχαλίδι καὶ ἁμαρτωλῷ, καὶ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐπαισχυνθήσεται αὐτὸν ὅταν ἔλθῃ ἐν τῇ δόξῃ τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτοῦ μετὰ τῶν ἀγγέλων τῶν ἁγίων.
records.gloss: Whoever for if is ashamed of me and my words in the generation this the adulterous and sinful, also the Son of Man will be ashamed of him, when he comes in the glory of the Father of him with the angels the holy.
pieces: Whoever is ashamed of {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} and of what I say, here among this adulterous, sinful generation, the Son of Man will in turn be ashamed of them, when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} comes with the holy angels in the glory of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Father."

L.38: For whoever is ashamed of {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} and of {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man also will be ashamed of {{gender:them|him}} when {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} comes in the glory of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Father with the holy angels."

R.38: The people of today have turned away from God and are full of sin. Among them, some people will be ashamed of {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} and of what I teach. When the Son of Man comes with the holy angels in the glory of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} Father, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will be ashamed of them."

decisions.choice: adulterous: unfaithful to God
decisions.reason: The prophets called Israel an adulterous wife when it turned to other gods (Hosea 2:2-5; Ezekiel 16:32). The word speaks of broken faith with God.

decisions.choice: ashamed of: refuse to own or stand by
decisions.reason: To be ashamed of Jesus is to disown him. The Son of Man will disown such a person in turn.

decisions.choice: the Son of Man comes in glory: the vision of Daniel 7:13-14
decisions.reason: One like a son of man comes with the clouds and receives glory and a kingdom. Jesus speaks of this again in 13:26 and 14:62.

decisions.choice: the glory of his Father: God's own glory, shown in the Son
decisions.reason: Jesus calls God his Father. The glory is God's own presence and splendor.

decisions.choice: the people of today have turned away from God and are full of sin
decisions.reason: Readable explains what adulterous means here and puts it in its own sentence.

decisions.choice: them
decisions.reason: As in 8:34, Balanced and Readable use them for a saying meant for anyone.
